source: CMS Provider Data Catalog, HCAHPS (Hospital Consumer Assessment of Healthcare Providers and Systems) — Hospital-level file, measure H_HSP_RATING_9_10 ("Overall Hospital Rating 9 or 10")
methodology: Percentile distribution (25th/50th/75th/90th) computed directly from CMS's published hospital-level HCAHPS microdata (n=3,949 individually-reporting hospitals), discharges 10/01/2024-09/30/2025. This exact percentile table is not published by CMS itself — CMS publishes only the per-hospital top-box percentages; the breakdown here was computed from that real data using standard percentile methodology. Cross-check: the computed median (72%) matches CMS's own separately-published national average (72%) for the same measure, confirmed directly against the CMS API.

source: CMS Hospital Readmissions Reduction Program (HRRP), FY2026 hospital-level file, Pneumonia 30-day risk-standardized readmission measure
methodology: CMS does not publish one blended all-cause readmission rate; HRRP data is condition-specific by design. Pneumonia was selected as the representative condition here (the largest reporting cohort of the 6 HRRP conditions, n=2,715 hospitals). p50 = median predicted readmission rate (15.5%); p90 = 90th-percentile rate (18.1%), i.e. among the worst-performing decile. Both computed directly from CMS's real hospital-level file, discharge period 07/01/2021-06/30/2024. Heart failure, AMI, COPD, CABG and hip/knee replacement each have their own, different readmission-rate distributions in the same file — this row reflects pneumonia only.

source: Leuchter et al., "Health Care Staffing Shortages and Potential National Hospital Bed Shortage," JAMA Network Open, Feb 2025
methodology: National mean hospital bed occupancy, May 2023-April 2024 (post-pandemic period), per mandatory HHS hospital capacity reporting cited in this peer-reviewed study. The same study cites a 2009-2019 baseline mean of 63.9% (sourced by the authors to AHA Hospital Statistics) — not used as a second percentile point here since it describes an earlier time period for the same national population, not a distribution across hospitals at one point in time. Single point only.

source: CMS "Timely and Effective Care" National dataset, measure OP-18b (median minutes in the ED before being seen by a provider, excluding psychiatric/transfer patients)
methodology: p50 = CMS's published national median (162 minutes), period 10/01/2024-09/30/2025. p25 = the "best decile" (~top 10% of hospitals) figure CMS's release describes as ~100 minutes — used here as a conservative approximation of the 25th percentile (the true 25th percentile is very likely somewhat higher than this best-decile figure, so this column understates rather than overstates how common a 100-minute wait is). Hospital ED-volume-tier breakdowns (low/medium/high/very-high annual visit volume: 123/165/202/201 min) were available but not used, since they stratify by hospital size rather than represent percentiles of the general population.
